column2: Some wars are of little fruit, or fruitless, or of doubtful fruit; some produce fault at present and are fruitless later;
some produce fault both later and at present — or one incited by another of unknown valor,
for another's sake, for a woman, for a long time with Brahmins, joined with untimely fate, and with a friend puffed up with strength:
one fruitful at present but fruitless later; one fruitful later but fruitless at present —
thus the sixteenfold war one should never make. The king should always perform action pure in both present and future.
Having considered the force glad and nourished, one should take the opposite course; when friend, Akranda and Asara are firmly devoted
and the enemy's are contrary, then one should wage war. Having made war, having made peace, and having united by occasion,
and by neglect, skilled ones remember the march as fivefold. Asana is remembered as from obstruction of each other's capacity;
of the enemy and the conqueror it is remembered fivefold like yana. Between two strong enemies, offering himself by speech,
he should stay in the dual policy, unnoticed like a crow's eye. In the clash of both he should serve the stronger;
when both, having made an agreement, do not wish union, then he should approach that enemy or go himself to the greater.
Being uprooted by the strong and lacking remedies, he should serve the family-exalted, truthful, noble and strong;
constant attendance on his sight, ever imbued with his sentiment, humility as he directs — the conduct of the refuge-seeker is heard.
Intoxication, heedlessness, desire and talk in sleep, and women hidden or sporting — these break counsel.
One bold, retentive, eloquent, firm in weapon and scripture, practiced in action deserves to be the king's envoy.
The one with full authority, the one with limited meaning, and the message-bearer — the envoy is remembered as threefold, each a quarter less in capacity.
He should not enter an unknown city of the enemy, nor one that praises; he should watch the time for the task and depart when permitted;
he should know the enemy's weak points, treasury, friends and forces; he should know affection and disaffection by looks, body and gestures.
He should make a fourfold praise of both sides. He should live with good spies in the guise of ascetics.
The open spy is the envoy; the unopen spy is twofold: merchant, farmer, one with marks, mendicant and the like are spies.
When envoys' efforts are fruitless he should march against an enemy in trouble; whatever trouble is natural, he should consider that and rise up;
because a man falls from the good by misconduct, therefore it is called trouble: fire, water, disease, famine and epidemic —
thus fivefold is divine trouble; the human is another. The divine one should be calmed by effort and propitiation;
the human trouble by policy with the risen. Counsel, attainment of its fruit, carrying out of tasks, the future,
income and expense, policy of punishment, repelling the enemy, remedy for trouble, protection of kingdom and king —
this is the minister's work; accompanied by trouble it destroys. Gold, grain, clothes and vehicle come from the subjects;
other heaps of wealth too; troubled subjects destroy. Protection of subjects in calamity, of treasury and army;
townsmen and others help by shelter here in bad days: silent war, saving the people, taking of friends and enemies;
feudatories and others, fault done, would perish by that trouble; maintenance of servants, giving, taking of subjects and friends,
divisions of dharma, desire and the rest, ornament of fort refurbishment: through trouble of the treasury it kills — the king is rooted in the treasury;
friends and enemies, land, gold, means, crushing the enemy, doing far work quickly — he loses by trouble of the army.
It supports friends and destroys the enemy; helpfulness with wealth and the rest — he loses by trouble of the friend.
A king in trouble destroys the king's affairs; harshness of speech and punishment and corruption of wealth,
drinking, women, hunting, dice — the troubles of the king; laziness, stiffness, pride, heedlessness, double-dealing:
thus the previously taught is remembered as the trouble of the minister. Drought and oppression and the like is called trouble of the kingdom;
broken machines, ramparts and moat, lack of weapons, a fort bound with a depleted army is called trouble of the fort;
spent, scattered, unreplenished, unsaved, spoiled and far-placed is called trouble of the treasury.
Besieged, scattered, dishonored and insulted, non-existent, sick, tired, come from far, newly come,
exhausted, repelled, struck at the front, full of hopelessness and despair, obtained through falsehood,
with wives and children cast in, with an inner thorn, with provisions and rear cut, empty at the root,
without a master, uncombined, with broken rank, with an evil rear-guard — this is called the trouble of the army.
A friend oppressed by fate and seized by the enemy's force, joined with desire, anger and the like, would be from effort by enemies.
Corruption of wealth arises from anger; harshness of speech and punishment; from desire: hunting, dice, drink and women — troubles.
Harshness of speech is the greatest in the world, causing agitation without purpose; punishment accomplishes the unaccomplished; the king should apply it with skill.
A king harsh in punishment agitates beings; beings, agitated, go to the enemies' refuge,
and the enemies, grown strong, become for his destruction. Abandonment of great wealth for corrupting the corruptible
is called corruption of wealth by knowers of the truth of policy. From drink loss of knowledge of what to do; from hunting destruction of the enemy;
for removing fatigue he may hunt in a protected forest. In dice loss of dharma, wealth, life and hopes, quarrels and the like;
from trouble of women comes loss of time and oppression of dharma and wealth; from the fault of drinking loss of life and of discernment of what is to be done.
One who knows camp-placement and omens conquers the enemy. In the middle of the camp, with the treasury, is the king's house;
the hereditary, guild, friendly, enemy and forest forces, having surrounded the royal palace, should be encamped in order.
A portion of the army, armed, led by the commander, should patrol the squares and the outer circle at night;
he should know the news of his own from those moving at far borders; all should go out and enter marked.
Conciliation, gift, division, punishment, neglect, jugglery and illusion — the seven means; one should apply them to the enemy for accomplishment.
Conciliation is remembered as fourfold: recounting services, telling mutual connection, speaking gently first,
sight at arrival, and offering by word "I am yours." Whatever giving of obtained wealth — best, worst or middling —
return gift, approval of what was taken, giving unprecedented wealth, and encouraging self-taking:
what is to be given and release — gift is remembered as fivefold. Removal of affection and attachment and production of delight,
and mutual division: division by knowers of division is remembered as threefold. Death, seizing wealth and harassment — punishment is threefold,
open and secret. People hating the openly hated... let the people be agitated by the slain; among them the lump is praised.
Especially by secret means one should kill enemies with weapons and the like. One should not kill a Brahmin merely by birth; one should control him with conciliation.
As if anointing minds, as if drinking at the sight of the good, as if swallowing nectar, one should use conciliation, pleasing speech.
One falsely accused, desiring prosperity, summoned and not honored, hating the king, over-taxed, and self-conceited,
one whose dharma, desire and wealth are cut off, angry, proud, insulted, abandoned without cause, even if made hostile, then conciliated,
one who lost wealth and wife, worthy of honor but not honored — these placed with the enemy, ever suspicious, one should divide;
those who come one should honor with desires and pacify one's own. Conciliation, joining the seen, showing extreme fear,
and giving chief honor are declared the means of division. A friend killed is like wood eaten by worms: it falls apart.
Possessing the three powers, knowing place and time, one should send enemies to destruction by punishment. One of kind intent, devoted to friendship, one should win by conciliation;
the greedy and the weakened by gifts; friends by mutual suspicion; the wicked by sight of punishment; sons, brothers and the like by conciliation;
army chiefs, warriors and country people by gifts and division; neighbors and foresters, the offenders, by division and punishment.
Images of deities are worshipped by men who are inside; a man at night wrapped in a woman's clothes, showing marvels,
imitating Vetala, meteors, Pishachas and jackal-women; taking shapes at will, raining weapons, fire, stones and water;
darkness, wind, fire, cloud — this is superhuman illusion. Bhima, adopting a woman's form, killed Kichaka.
Non-prevention of one engaged in an unjust act, trouble or war is called neglect; the brother (Bhima) was neglected by Hidimba.
